title: The Sword Against the Philistines
summary: A short poem announces disaster on the Philistine cities of the coast. Floodwaters rise from the north, chariots thunder, and fathers flee without looking back for their children; Gaza and Ashkelon go into mourning. The chapter ends with a cry to the sword of the LORD to rest and the answer that it cannot rest while the LORD has given it a task.
story: This is the second of the oracles concerning the nations, after Egypt in chapter 46. The Philistines were among Israel's oldest neighbors and rivals, from the days of the judges, Samson, and Saul to David's victories over them. By Jeremiah's time they were a group of city-states on the southern coast, squeezed between the great powers of Egypt and Mesopotamia. The chapter continues the collection's theme that the God of Israel rules the fate of every nation. Its closing dialogue with the sword gives voice to the pain of judgment even while affirming that God commands it. Chapter 48 turns east to Moab.
historical:
The heading dates the oracle “before Pharaoh struck down Gaza” (verse 1), but it doesn't say which pharaoh or when. Several dates have been proposed. Pharaoh Neco II campaigned along the coast around 609 BC, and the Greek historian Herodotus mentions him taking a city called Kadytis, which many identify with Gaza. Neco may also have attacked Gaza around 601 BC, after the Egyptians turned back a Babylonian army at their border. Others suggest a later pharaoh such as Hophra. The poem itself says the disaster comes from the north, which fits the Babylonian armies.

The Babylonian Chronicle records that in the winter of 604 BC, in the month of Kislev, Nebuchadnezzar marched to Ashkelon, captured it, took its king prisoner, and destroyed the city. Excavations at Ashkelon led by Lawrence Stager uncovered a thick destruction layer from that time, with collapsed buildings and signs of violent death, which the excavators linked to Nebuchadnezzar's attack. An Aramaic letter found at Saqqara in Egypt, written by a coastal king named Adon asking Pharaoh for help against an approaching Babylonian army, probably dates from these years, though the identity of Adon's city is uncertain.
cultural:
The Philistines were one of the Sea Peoples who settled on the southern coast of Canaan around the twelfth century BC. Their five main cities were Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath. The Old Testament traces their origin to Caphtor (verse 4; Amos 9:7), usually identified with Crete or the wider Aegean world, and archaeology has found strong Aegean influence in early Philistine pottery and customs. Tyre and Sidon, the great Phoenician ports to the north, were their trading partners and possible allies.

The mourning practices in verse 5, shaving the head and gashing the skin, were common in the region; the law of Moses forbade Israelites to practice them for the dead (Deuteronomy 14:1). The image in verse 3 of fathers too terrified to turn back for their children was a picture of total panic, as the bonds of family give way before the enemy. The rising waters from the north (verse 2) echo the flood imagery of 46:7-8, now turned against Egypt's neighbors.
literary: The poem is brief and intense. It opens with an image of floodwaters rising, moves quickly to the sounds of battle (hooves, chariots, wheels), then to the human cost, and finally to mourning. The last two verses form a dialogue: someone, perhaps the prophet or the Philistines themselves, cries out to the sword of the LORD, “how long until you rest?” (verse 6), and the answer comes that the sword cannot rest while the LORD has commanded it (verse 7). This way of speaking to an object, called apostrophe, makes the sword almost a living agent. The question “how long” echoes the laments of the Psalms. The repetition of remnant (verses 4 and 5) suggests that the Philistines had already suffered much and that this would finish what remained.

outline.t: The flood from the north and the terror of battle
A cry to the sword of the LORD

doctrines.note: The sword that falls on the Philistines is “the sword of the LORD” (verse 6), commanded and appointed by him. The armies of the nations, even when they don't know it, carry out his purposes.
The judgment on the Philistines is total, cutting off even their allies. Yet the chapter's final lament shows that judgment is not a matter for rejoicing; even the sword's work is grievous.
The poem lingers on human anguish: wailing, fathers unable to save their sons, mourning rites. Scripture does not hide the cost of judgment, even on Israel's old enemies.

words.note: Cherev, sword. The sword appears throughout Jeremiah as an instrument of judgment, often with famine and plague. Here it is personified as the sword of the LORD, addressed as if it could hear and answer.

Shaqat, to be quiet or at rest. The cry “cease and be still” (verse 6) uses this verb, and verse 7 asks how the sword can rest. The same word describes the land having rest in the book of Judges after God delivers his people.

Kaphtor, Caphtor, the land the Philistines came from, usually identified with Crete or the Aegean region. Mentioning it recalls that the Philistines were once newcomers, brought to Canaan, as Amos 9:7 says, by the same God who brought Israel out of Egypt.

Tsavah, to command or give an order. God has commanded the sword (verse 7), and it cannot rest until its task is done. The verb is the same one used for God's commands to Israel, showing that his authority extends over every power.

christ: The chapter ends with a cry to the sword of the LORD to return to its sheath. The New Testament records Jesus telling Peter to put his sword back in its place on the night of his arrest (Matthew 26:52), and Christians have seen in the cross the place where God's judgment against sin fell once for all. The New Testament doesn't connect this chapter to Christ directly, so the link is thematic. The lament of verse 6, asking how long until the sword rests, finds an answer in the gospel's promise that in Christ God has made peace, and in the prophets' hope of a day when swords are beaten into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4). Even the Philistines are within the reach of that hope: Zechariah 9:7 pictures a remnant of them belonging to God.

hard.q: The heading mentions Pharaoh striking Gaza, but the poem speaks of an enemy from the north. Do the two fit together?
hard.a: Interpreters answer this in different ways. One view is that the heading only dates the oracle, telling us when Jeremiah spoke it (before an Egyptian attack on Gaza), while the poem predicts a different disaster to come later from the north, meaning Babylon. On this view the destruction of Ashkelon in 604 BC is a likely fulfillment. Another view is that the northern enemy could describe an army coming down the coast from Syria, which Egypt's army also did when returning from campaigns in the north, so the heading and poem may describe related events. Some scholars suggest the heading was added later by an editor. The text does not settle the question, and the poem's main point, that the Philistine cities would fall under God's judgment, stands on any reading.

questions: The poem pictures fathers so terrified they cannot turn back for their children. What does this tell us about the human cost of war?
Someone cries out to the sword of the LORD, how long until you rest? When have you longed for a season of judgment or suffering to end?
The Philistines were Israel's ancient enemies, yet the chapter grieves their fall. How should God's people respond to the suffering of those who have opposed them?
